cards.front: What is the fundamental microscopic origin of surface tension in a liquid?
cards.back: Surface tension arises from the imbalance of intermolecular cohesive forces at the liquid-gas (or liquid-liquid) interface. Molecules in the bulk are attracted equally in all directions, but surface molecules experience a net inward attractive force from the bulk molecules, leading to a tendency to minimize surface area and an associated surface energy.

cards.front: Define surface tension ($\gamma$) in terms of both energy and force, including its standard SI units.
cards.back:
• Energy definition: Surface tension is the excess potential energy per unit area of the surface, measured in Joules per square meter ($J/m^2$).
  • Force definition: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting parallel to the surface and perpendicular to a line drawn on the surface, measured in Newtons per meter ($N/m$).
These units are equivalent ($J/m^2 = (N \cdot m)/m^2 = N/m$).

cards.front: State the general form of the Young-Laplace equation for the pressure difference ($\Delta P$) across a curved fluid interface, defining all variables.
cards.back:
The Young-Laplace equation is: $$ \Delta P = P_{inside} - P_{outside} = \gamma \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right) $$ Where:
  • $\Delta P$: Pressure difference across the interface.
  • $\gamma$: Surface tension of the fluid.
  • $R_1, R_2$: The two principal radii of curvature of the interface at a given point. By convention, radii are positive if the center of curvature is on the "inside" (higher pressure side) of the interface.

cards.front: How does the Young-Laplace equation simplify for a perfectly spherical liquid droplet of radius $R$?
cards.back:
For a spherical droplet, both principal radii of curvature are equal to the radius of the sphere ($R_1 = R_2 = R$).
The equation simplifies to:
$$ \Delta P = \frac{2\gamma}{R} $$
This means the pressure inside a spherical droplet is higher than the pressure outside.

cards.front: Explain the difference in the Young-Laplace equation application for a spherical liquid droplet versus a spherical soap bubble, both of radius $R$.
cards.back:
• Spherical Liquid Droplet: Has only one air-liquid interface. The pressure difference is $\Delta P = \frac{2\gamma}{R}$.
  • Spherical Soap Bubble: Consists of a thin liquid film with two air-liquid interfaces (inner and outer). Each interface contributes to the pressure difference. Therefore, the total pressure difference between the inside of the bubble and the outside air is $\Delta P = 2 \times \frac{2\gamma}{R} = \frac{4\gamma}{R}$.

cards.front: Using a force balance approach, derive the Young-Laplace equation for a spherical interface of radius $R$.
cards.back:
Consider a hypothetical plane cutting a spherical interface (e.g., a droplet) into two hemispheres. The pressure difference $\Delta P$ acts on the circular cross-section of area $\pi R^2$, creating an outward force $F_P = \Delta P \cdot \pi R^2$. The surface tension $\gamma$ acts along the circumference of the cut, pulling inwards. The total inward force from surface tension is $F_S = \gamma \cdot (2\pi R)$.
At equilibrium, these forces balance:
$$ F_P = F_S $$
$$ \Delta P \cdot \pi R^2 = \gamma \cdot 2\pi R $$
$$ \Delta P = \frac{2\pi R \gamma}{\pi R^2} $$
$$ \Delta P = \frac{2\gamma}{R} $$

cards.front: Why does a smaller soap bubble require a higher internal pressure to prevent collapse compared to a larger one?
cards.back: According to the Young-Laplace equation for a soap bubble, $\Delta P = \frac{4\gamma}{R}$. This equation shows that the pressure difference across the bubble wall ($\Delta P$) is inversely proportional to the radius $R$. As the radius $R$ decreases, the term $\frac{4\gamma}{R}$ increases, meaning a larger pressure difference is required to balance the increased curvature-induced surface tension forces. Thus, a smaller bubble must have a higher internal pressure relative to its surroundings.
